newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Analysts hope to see Australian jobs data.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Analysts hope to see Australian jobs data.

text.p: Australian economists would like to see the unemployment figures that the official statistician is monitoring for effects of a new sampling methodology.
"We would be interested to see the two sets of numbers," said John Kyriakopoulos, senior economist at Macquarie Bank.
The Australian Bureau of Statistics says results from its new telephone interviews, which are being progressively introduced, are not noticeably different to those collected face-to-face.
Differential results would distort the rates of change in the data during the change-over period.

But sources familiar with the data say the bureau has noticed an impact. The first few months of telephone interviewing produced an unemployment rate about half a percentage point higher than the old method, although later data suggested a narrower but still positive impact, they say.
A spokesman said on Thursday that by "noticeable" the bureau meant "statistically significant."
However, the bureau has refused to issue the numerical results of its internal monitoring. On Wednesday, following a report of the sources' assertions, it repeated its established assurance.
"At this point in time, after the four-month period August to November, no noticeable effect on the unemployment rate for each of the months has been detected," the bureau said on Wednesday.
"This is clearly good news and I am sure it must be true," responded Bankers Trust chief economist Chris Caton.
"But it would be interesting to see the sample arithmetic for the months of August through November."
Asked why the bureau would not issue the figures, a spokesman said: "They are part of our internal monitoring process.
"No real advantage would be served in publicising the details of that process."
The bureau is one of the world's most highly regarded official statisticians.
Analysts surveyed by The Economist business magazine in 1991 rated it second in the world after its Canadian equivalent.
The bureau will have only the phase-in period to monitor any impact of telephone interviewing and will have no way at all to identify any seasonal impact of the change-over.
The bureau's monthly population survey, which produces labour force data, works on a sample divided into eight panels, each of about 8,000 people.
Each month the bureau replaces a panel and since August every new panel has been interviewed by telephone.
Accordingly there will be seven months -- August to February -- in which a comparison of the two methods can be made.
In March, the eighth month, no panels will be interviewed face-to-face.
The bureau says that its "no noticeable impact" statement will be reviewed with each month's data.
The next labour force release is due on January 16.
